I will use `waterways` as an instrument for the segregation index. The program documentation reveals that boundary streams from a 1920 survey created jurisdiction lines, leading to higher fragmentation and, as noted, higher segregation indices. The instrument is `credit_waiver`, as it was randomly assigned and increased the probability of graduation without affecting other aspects of the participants' lives. The treatment variable is high school graduation by age 19, and the outcome is whether the participant voted in at least one general election from 1998 to 2008. The first-stage regression will relate the waiver to graduation, and the second-stage will relate graduation to voter turnout. The main threat to identification is the potential for a weak instrument, as the first-stage F-statistic is reported to be approximately 2. I will use an instrumental variables (IV) approach to estimate the causal effect of schooling on log weekly wages. The identification strategy relies on quarter-of-birth (`qob1`) as an instrument for years of completed schooling, exploiting the interaction between school-entry laws and compulsory schooling laws that allow students to drop out on their 16th birthday. Men born in the first quarter of the year enter school later and are thus closer to their 16th birthday when they reach the final grade, leading to fewer completed years of schooling on average. This provides a source of exogenous variation in education that is not correlated with innate ability. The primary threat to identification is the possibility that births in the first quarter are disproportionately associated with familial characteristics (e.g., teenage or unmarried mothers) that independently affect earnings.

The first stage will regress years of completed schooling on `qob1` and the fixed effects, while the second stage will regress log weekly wage on the predicted schooling.
